notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 2 Kings 2, drawn from the sources found.

---

## 2 Kings 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v. 1

**Traditional Reading:**
- The chapter opens with a heading that anticipates the whole story: God was about to take Elijah to heaven by a whirlwind. The event is presented as God's sovereign initiative, not Elijah's choice. The Hebrew verb *hayah* ("and it came about") signals a divinely appointed moment.
  — [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-2-commentary)
- Elijah and Elisha set out from Gilgal. This is not the well-known Gilgal near Jericho (below sea level) but a Gilgal in the hill country of Ephraim, about seven miles north of Bethel (around 2,800 feet elevation). This explains why v. 2 says they "went down" to Bethel.
  — [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-2-commentary) | [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Gilgal, Bethel, and Jericho each had schools or guilds of the prophets. Elijah was visiting these communities as a farewell tour before his departure.
  — [JFB / Blue Letter Bible](https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_002.cfm)
- The knowledge of Elijah's coming departure was apparently widespread — Elijah, Elisha, and the sons of the prophets all knew.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

**Other Views:**
- Ellicott notes the LXX renders "into heaven" as "as into heaven" (ὡς εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν), perhaps to suggest that not the visible heavens but God Himself was the real goal.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)

---

### vv. 2–3

**Traditional Reading:**
- Elijah tells Elisha to stay at Gilgal because the LORD has sent him to Bethel. This is widely seen as a test of Elisha's devotion, not a dismissal. Elijah gives Elisha three opportunities to turn back (Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho), and each time Elisha refuses. True calling is confirmed through perseverance.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-2-commentary)
- **Ellicott offers a different view:** Elijah was not testing Elisha but was genuinely uncertain whether God willed Elisha to accompany him. Elisha's threefold refusal settled the doubt. (Comp. John 21:15ff.)
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Elisha's oath — "As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives" — is a doubly solemn oath, more emphatic than either phrase alone.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- The "sons of the prophets" at Bethel came out to Elisha (not Elijah), suggesting Elisha walked ahead to announce his master. They too knew supernaturally that Elijah would be taken "today."
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- "From thy head" — an allusion to the custom of a master sitting higher than disciples who sat at his feet (cf. Acts 22:3).
  — [JFB / Blue Letter Bible](https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_002.cfm) | [Trapp](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-kings-2.html)
- Elisha's reply "Yes, I know; keep silent!" (or "hush!") reflects grief, not secrecy. The Hebrew *hehĕshû* imitates the sound of "hush." The subject was painful to him.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm) | [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

---

### vv. 4–7

**Traditional Reading:**
- The same pattern repeats at Jericho (vv. 4–5) and the Jordan (vv. 6–7). At each stage Elijah says "Stay here," and Elisha refuses. The threefold repetition echoes other biblical testing patterns (e.g., Peter's threefold denial and restoration).
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Trapp](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-kings-2.html)
- The "fifty men of the sons of the prophets" stood at a distance opposite them by the Jordan. They wanted to witness what would happen. Constable notes these fifty may have been attendants or younger members of the prophetic guild.
  — [JFB / Blue Letter Bible](https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_002.cfm) | [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-2.html)
- F. B. Meyer (quoted in Enduring Word): "The prophet's evident desire to die alone shames us, when we remember how eager we are to tell men, by every available medium, of what we are doing for the Lord."
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

---

### v. 8

**Traditional Reading:**
- Elijah took his mantle (the hairy *addereth* that marked him as prophet, cf. Zech 13:4), rolled it up, and struck the Jordan. The waters parted, and they crossed on dry ground.
- This miracle deliberately echoes Moses parting the Red Sea (Ex 14) and Joshua parting the Jordan (Josh 3–4). It demonstrates that the same God who led Israel out of Egypt and into Canaan is still at work through His prophet.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [JFB / Blue Letter Bible](https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_002.cfm)
- The mantle, like Moses' rod, was a visible channel of invisible spiritual power — an outward sign operated by faith.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)

---

### vv. 9–10

**Traditional Reading:**
- After crossing, Elijah gives Elisha an open invitation: "Ask what I shall do for you." Elisha has proved his devotion and now receives what amounts to a blank cheque.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)
- Elisha asks for "a double portion of your spirit." This does **not** mean twice the spiritual power of Elijah. It refers to the portion of the firstborn son under Mosaic law (Deut 21:17), who received a double share of the inheritance. Elisha was asking to be recognised as Elijah's true spiritual heir and successor — the firstborn among the "sons of the prophets."
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm) | [JFB / Blue Letter Bible](https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_002.cfm)
- Ellicott adds a nuance: Elisha asks to receive twice the share of any other "son of the prophets," not twice what Elijah himself had. The phrase "a mouth of two" may come from the custom of serving honoured guests double portions (Gen 43:34).
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Elijah replies, "You have asked a hard thing." This was hard because only God — not Elijah — could grant spiritual power. Elijah sets a condition: "If you see me as I am taken from you, it shall be so."
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)

**Typological Reading (Grant's / Brethren):**
- Elisha is seen as a type of Christ. Elijah (like John the Baptist) gives way to one with a "double portion" — the two-fold ministry of grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). Elijah's ascension prefigures Christ's ascension and the sending of the Spirit.
  — [Grant's Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-kings-2.html)

---

### v. 11

**Traditional Reading:**
- As they walked and talked, a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated them. Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
- **Important distinction:** The whirlwind took Elijah up, not the chariot. The chariot and horses of fire "separated the two of them" (came between them). Many popular depictions (e.g., William Blake's painting) incorrectly show Elijah riding the chariot into heaven.
  — [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-2-commentary) | [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- The fiery chariot and horses symbolize God's powerful heavenly army — the same imagery Elisha will later see in 2 Kings 6:17 when his servant's eyes are opened to the angelic hosts.
  — [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-2.html)
- Constable notes the polemic value: the Canaanites called Baal "the rider of clouds"; here Yahweh, not Baal, rides the storm.
  — [Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-2.html)
- Ellicott cautions against an overly literal reading: in Hebrew thought, the thunder-cloud was God's chariot, thunder His voice, lightning His arrow (Ps 18:6–15; Ps 104:3). The essential meaning is that God suddenly took Elijah to Himself amid a grand display of power in nature.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):**
- Spurgeon preached on this verse (Oct 1865), treating Elijah's departure as a type of the sudden death of believers. He notes the paradox: death is both terrible (horses and chariots of fire) and triumphant (riding to heaven). "To die is triumph to the Christian."
  — [Spurgeon](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-kings-2.html)

---

### v. 12

**Traditional Reading:**
- Elisha saw it — fulfilling the condition of v. 10. He cried out, "My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!"
- "My father" expresses the spiritual father–son relationship between Elijah and Elisha. "The chariots and horsemen of Israel" means Elijah was worth more to Israel's defence than all its military forces. His prayers and prophetic ministry were the nation's true protection.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Elisha tore his clothes in two — the traditional sign of extreme grief. This was genuine mourning, not just symbolic.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):**
- Spurgeon: "You may weep, for 'Jesus wept.' Do not think there is any sin in sorrowing over departed friends." But grief should be moderated; there is a point where grief becomes rebellion against God.
  — [Spurgeon](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-kings-2.html)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):**
- G. Campbell Morgan (quoted): "Elisha saw that the strength of Israel had been that of the presence of the prophet of God." When Elisha himself later died, King Joash used the same words (2 Kings 13:14).
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

---

### vv. 13–14

**Traditional Reading:**
- Elisha picked up Elijah's fallen mantle. The mantle was the distinctive mark of the prophetic office; picking it up symbolised accepting the succession.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Elisha struck the Jordan with the mantle and cried, "Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" This question was not despair but faith: Elisha knew the power was in God, not in the mantle. If the same God was with him, the same power would follow.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-2-commentary)
- The waters parted, confirming publicly that Elisha had inherited Elijah's ministry and God's power was with him.

**Baptist (Spurgeon):**
- "And when you have got their mantle, do not waste precious time in lamentations about them any more; get to your business. There is a river in your way; what then? Well, go to the Jordan as the prophet Elisha did… Say not, 'Where is Elijah?' but 'Where is the Lord God of Elijah?' Elijah is gone, but his God is not."
  — [Spurgeon](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-kings-2.html) (quoted in Enduring Word)

---

### v. 15

**Traditional Reading:**
- The sons of the prophets at Jericho saw Elisha repeat Elijah's miracle and declared, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." They bowed to the ground before him, acknowledging him as their new head.
- This recognition was based on deeds, not words. Elisha did not need to argue for his legitimacy; God's power demonstrated it.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)
- Ellicott: "The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha" — the Hebrew verb means "hath alighted, settled, rested." The proof was the repeated miracle.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)

---

### vv. 16–18

**Traditional Reading:**
- The sons of the prophets propose sending fifty strong men to search for Elijah, suggesting the Spirit may have cast him onto some mountain or into a valley. This shows they did not fully grasp that Elijah had been taken permanently to heaven. They may have thought it was like the Spirit transporting Philip (Acts 8:39–40).
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm) | [JFB / Blue Letter Bible](https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_002.cfm)
- Elisha initially refuses ("Do not send them") but they press him until he is ashamed, and he relents. The fifty search for three days and find nothing.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Elisha's final words, "Did I not tell you not to go?", reinforce his authority and the lesson that God's word through His prophet is reliable. The close of Elijah's history teaches, as Reuss (quoted by Ellicott) notes, that the disciples must not seek their departed master in the desert but find among themselves the means of carrying on his work.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)

---

### vv. 19–22

**Traditional Reading:**
- The men of Jericho (ordinary citizens, not the prophets) approach Elisha with a practical problem: the city is beautifully situated, but the water is bad and the land suffers miscarriages (the Hebrew literally means the land "causes to miscarry" or is "barren" — referring to infertility in livestock and people, not just crop failure).
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm) | [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)
- Elisha calls for a **new** bowl with salt. The new bowl symbolises something uncontaminated, set apart for a holy purpose (cf. Num 19:2; 2 Sam 6:3). Salt, as an antiseptic/preservative, was a fitting sacramental sign of the purification God would work.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Elisha went to the spring itself (the source, not the streams) and cast the salt in, declaring, "Thus says the LORD: 'I have healed this water.'" The healing was God's act, announced by prophetic word, not a natural effect of the salt.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)
- "The waters remain healed to this day" — a note from the time the narrative was first written down, indicating a lasting, verifiable miracle.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
- Trapp: "If God casteth into our hearts but one cruseful of the salt of his Spirit, we are whole."
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

**Reformed / Typological (Grant):**
- This healing miracle (grace) paired with the later judgment (v. 23–24) sets the tone for Elisha's whole ministry: blessing to the needy and judgment on those who reject Yahweh. The "double portion" is seen in these two complementary aspects.
  — [Grant's Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-kings-2.html)

---

### vv. 23–25

**Traditional Reading:**
- Elisha goes up to Bethel (a centre of Jeroboam's calf-worship, 1 Kings 12:28–29). A group comes out and mocks him: "Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!"
- **Who were they?** The Hebrew *na'ar* (translated "youths," "boys," or "little children" in older versions like KJV) is a broad term. It is used of Joseph at age 30 (Gen 41:46), Absalom as an adult (2 Sam 14:21), and Solomon at 20 (1 Kings 3:7). These were not small children but young men — likely late teens or early twenties.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [GotQuestions (search result)](https://www.gotquestions.org/Elisha-baldhead.html)
- **What did the taunt mean?** "Go up" mocked Elijah's ascension — "Why don't you go up to heaven like your master did?" It was not teasing about baldness; it was blasphemous mockery of God's miraculous work. The repetition ("Go up… Go up") suggests a chant. They were from Bethel, the centre of calf-worship, and likely represented organised opposition to Yahweh's prophet.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Gaebelein](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-kings-2.html) | [GotQuestions (search result)](https://www.gotquestions.org/Elisha-baldhead.html)
- **The curse and bears:** Elisha turned, looked at them, and pronounced a curse "in the name of the LORD." Two female bears came out of the woods and "mauled" forty-two of them. The Hebrew verb means "to cut up" or "tear." It does not necessarily mean they were killed — the word can indicate serious but non-fatal injuries.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)
- **Why so severe?** Several points from the sources:
  - The group was large (forty-two were struck, implying the mob was even larger) and may have been dangerously threatening. Elisha may have needed divine intervention to escape.
  - The mockery was directed not merely at a bald man but at God's prophet, his predecessor's miraculous ascension, and ultimately at God Himself.
  - Bethel was the headquarters of idolatry. These youths likely represented organised, idolatrous opposition to the true worship of Yahweh.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/) | [Gaebelein](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-kings-2.html) | [Church Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/2-kings-2.html)
- The chapter ends with Elisha going to Mount Carmel (Elijah's place of triumph) and then to Samaria (the capital), signalling the beginning of his public ministry.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

**Gaebelein (Dispensational):**
- This was not disproportionate to the offence. The young men had scoffed at the power of God. Present-day mockers of the gospel will also receive punishment in due time (2 Peter 3:3–7).
  — [Gaebelein](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-kings-2.html)

---

## Denominational Distinctives & Other Views

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- Emphasis on the "double portion" as spiritual power for ministry and the necessity of actively "picking up the mantle" — believers must decide to take on the calling. Elisha's question "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" is a model for asking where God's power is in our work.
  — [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-2/)

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
- Focus on the practical, devotional application: prepare for death by working till the last moment ("die in harness"); when godly people die, pick up their mantle (their example) and carry on. "Say not, 'Where is Elijah?' but 'Where is the Lord God of Elijah?'"
  — [Spurgeon](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-kings-2.html)

### Reformed / Presbyterian (JFB)
- Notes the event was "a visible proof of another state, and a type of the resurrection of Christ." The revelation of Elijah's translation to so many was "a necessary part of the dispensation" under the law.
  — [JFB / Blue Letter Bible](https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_002.cfm)

### Brethren / Typological (Grant)
- The entire chapter is read christologically: Elijah = John the Baptist; Elisha = Christ (and Christ in the believer). The double portion = grace and truth. The mantle = the Holy Spirit given after Christ's ascension. Healing Jericho and judging Bethel = the two sides of Christ's ministry.
  — [Grant's Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-kings-2.html)

### Modern Scholarship Notes
- Ellicott (19th-century critical scholarship) notes the narrative likely originated in oral tradition in the prophetic guilds, as suggested by the exact repetition in vv. 2–6. He also urges caution about taking the fiery chariot "in too literal a sense," seeing it as Hebrew poetic imagery for God's presence in storm phenomena.
  — [Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/2.htm)
